passage:
“Parveen, can you do the deck for tomorrow?” Varun said at 5 pm, already reaching for his coat.
“Which deck? For whom?”
“The one for the meeting. You know.”
“Do you want the numbers from last quarter?”
“Yes, something like that. Don't take too long.”
Parveen stayed till eight, guessing at the order and adding charts. The next morning, Varun clicked through and frowned. “Why is this so long? I said keep it simple.”
“You said something like that,” Parveen answered quietly, and did not say more.
On Friday Parveen began checking every small choice three times, and stopped taking any task without written details.

qa.q: At what time did Varun ask Parveen for the deck?
qa.a: Varun asked Parveen for the deck at 5 pm.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel after Varun's frown on the second morning?
qa.a: Parveen feels set up to fail, hurt and quietly frustrated, since the task came without context or standards.

qa.q: What could Varun have told Parveen when handing over the deck?
qa.a: Varun could have said who the meeting is with, what matters most, how many slides, and the deadline.

qa.q: What might Varun be thinking when he frowns and says “I said keep it simple”?
qa.a: Varun probably believes the instruction was clear and is disappointed at the result, without seeing that the gap was in what was said.

grounding: A junior gets a task without context, priority or the standard expected, guesses, and is criticised afterwards.

passage: My first job taught me caution the hard way. Joseph, my senior, tossed me a sentence one Thursday: “Sort out the inventory file.” No deadline, no explanation of what “sort out” meant, no idea whether anyone else needed it. I guessed: I deleted duplicates and rearranged columns. On Monday, Joseph opened it and went quiet, then said, “You removed the old codes. We need those for the audit.” My stomach dropped. Nobody had said so. For months afterwards I sent questions about every tiny thing, and hesitated before touching any file, because I now felt every task might be a trap. I learned to ask, but the fear stayed longer. — Sahil

qa.q: What did Joseph say to Sahil that Thursday?
qa.a: Joseph said, “Sort out the inventory file.”

qa.q: What did Sahil feel when Joseph said the old codes were needed?
qa.a: Sahil's stomach dropped: Sahil felt set up to fail and afraid, since nobody had said the codes mattered.

qa.q: What could Sahil have asked on Thursday to avoid the mistake?
qa.a: Ask what sort out means, who will use the file, what must not be removed and when it is needed.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen the task Joseph handed over?
qa.a: Joseph may have thought the request was obvious and small, and was probably surprised and irritated, without realising the missing context.

grounding: A junior receives a task without context, priority or standard, guesses, is criticised and becomes more cautious.

passage:
Uday: my manager just said "clean up the customer list" and left for a meeting
Tanvir: clean up how?
Uday: no idea. remove duplicates? fix spellings? delete old customers?
Tanvir: ask?
Uday: he's in meetings till 6. and he hates being disturbed
Tanvir: so what'll you do
Uday: guess I guess
(Next day)
Uday: he's upset. I deleted inactive customers, he wanted them kept
Tanvir: but he never said that
Uday: he said "anyone would know"
Tanvir: that's not fair
Uday: I feel like I was set up to fail 😔
Uday: next time I'm not touching anything till I get it in writing
Tanvir: or ask him 3 questions before starting: why, by when, what does good look like
Uday: yeah. that's better than hiding

qa.q: What did Uday delete from the customer list?
qa.a: Uday deleted inactive customers.

qa.q: How did Uday feel after the manager was upset?
qa.a: Uday felt set up to fail and discouraged, since the manager had never said what was wanted.

qa.q: What could Uday do next time a task is unclear?
qa.a: Ask three questions before starting: why, by when and what good looks like, rather than guessing or freezing.

qa.q: How does Tanvir see the manager's criticism?
qa.a: Tanvir sees it as unfair, because the manager never gave the needed context.

grounding: A chat shows a junior given a task with no context or standard, guessing, and feeling set up to fail when criticised.

passage: Ira, twenty-three, had just started as an assistant at a small tourism office in Hampi. On Friday her boss, Vaibhav, handed her a folder. "Make something for the new visitors." He left for Bengaluru. Ira didn't know if he meant a brochure, a map or a website page; whether it was urgent; or who the visitors were. She chose a brochure and spent the weekend on it. On Monday he flipped through it and frowned. "I meant a one-page map for the hotel desks. This is too long." Ira's cheeks burned. That evening she wrote a list of questions to ask before starting any task. The next week, when he gave her a task, she asked all of them first, a little stiffly.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav say he meant after seeing the brochure?
qa.a: He meant a one-page map for the hotel desks.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when Vaibhav frowned at the brochure?
qa.a: Her cheeks burned; she felt embarrassed and unfairly judged, since she had been given no details.

qa.q: What did Ira do next, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She wrote a list of questions to ask before any task, which gets the context and standard up front.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Ira's new habit of asking questions?
qa.a: Vaibhav might find it a little stiff at first, but it will save him from wasted work and disappointment.

grounding: Shows a junior given a vague task who guesses, is criticised, and becomes more cautious.

passage: Hana had been at the marketing agency in Seoul for two months when her team leader, Chen, messaged: "Please handle the client's social media this week." No priority, no tone, no examples. Hana checked old posts, guessed a friendly style and posted twice a day. On Friday Chen called her in. "The client wanted formal posts. And only three this week." Hana nodded, heart pounding, and apologised. She didn't point out that nobody had told her. The next week, when Chen gave her another task, she hesitated for so long before starting that she missed the first deadline. Being wrong once had made her afraid to move at all.

qa.q: How many posts did the client want that week?
qa.a: The client wanted only three this week.

qa.q: How did Hana feel on Friday when Chen called her in?
qa.a: Hana felt anxious, with her heart pounding, and blamed herself though she hadn't been told.

qa.q: What would have helped Hana at the start?
qa.a: Chen stating the priority, tone and number of posts, or Hana asking about them before posting.

qa.q: How might Chen see Hana's hesitation the next week?
qa.a: Chen might see it as slowness, not realising that the unclear first task and criticism made Hana cautious.

grounding: Shows a junior given a task without priority or standard, criticised afterwards, and becoming more hesitant.

passage: At the community centre in Ludhiana, Gurleen stopped at Akash's desk on her way to a meeting. "Make something for Senior Citizens' Day, na? You'll manage." No date, no idea of what "something" meant. Akash, three weeks into the job, guessed. He spent two days designing a colourful quiz on old Punjabi film songs, printed thirty copies and laminated a sign. On Thursday Gurleen looked at it and frowned. "I needed the programme schedule for the notice board. And this print is too small for them to read. Didn't you think?" Akash said sorry and took the sheets back. That evening he stared at the unused quizzes, feeling foolish and set up. The next week, when she asked him to "fix the attendance sheet", he emailed her four questions before touching it and waited a whole day for her answers.

qa.q: How many copies of the quiz did Akash print?
qa.a: Thirty copies.

qa.q: How did Akash feel that evening, and why?
qa.a: He felt foolish and set up to fail, because he had guessed at a vague request in good faith and was then criticised for not reading Gurleen's mind.

qa.q: How could Gurleen hand over the next task more clearly?
qa.a: She could say what the thing is for, when it is due and what a good result looks like, for example a large-print programme schedule for the notice board by Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Akash's four-question email the next week?
qa.a: Gurleen may find it slow or fussy without realising her own vague request and sharp comment are what made him so cautious.

grounding: Shows a junior who guesses at a task given without context or standard, is criticised afterwards, and becomes much more cautious.
